characterList.description: An unseen male instructor provides the narration throughout the video.

content_metadata.description: This video is a chemistry lesson focused on drawing Lewis structures of molecules and introducing the concept of resonance.

qAndA.answer: Formaldehyde (H2CO) contributes a total of 12 valence electrons. (Scene 2, 01:25)
qAndA.question: How many valence electrons does formaldehyde contribute in total?

qAndA.answer: A triple bond is required between carbon and nitrogen in hydrogen cyanide. (Scene 3, 02:31)
qAndA.question: How many bonds are required between carbon and nitrogen in hydrogen cyanide to satisfy the octet rule?

qAndA.answer: A negative charge adds an electron to the total valence electron count. (Scene 4, 02:51)
qAndA.question: Does a negative charge on a polyatomic ion add or remove an electron from the total valence electron count?

qAndA.answer: Resonance is the term for this phenomenon. (Scene 5, 03:54)
qAndA.question: What term describes the phenomenon where multiple valid Lewis structures can be drawn for a molecule?

qAndA.answer: No, ozone does not have distinct short double and long single bonds. The real molecule is a hybrid of the resonance structures, resulting in bonds with intermediate lengths. (Scene 5, 04:40-04:45)
qAndA.question: Does ozone have a short double bond and a long single bond?

activities.description: The instructor demonstrates drawing the Lewis structure for the nitrate ion (NO3-), highlighting the influence of the negative charge on the total valence electrons and the requirement for a double bond.
The instructor introduces the possibility of multiple correct structures due to the choice of oxygen atom for the double bond.

mood.description: The introduction of multiple possible structures adds complexity and encourages further investigation into the concept of resonance.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene introduces polyatomic ions and their Lewis structures, emphasizing the impact of charge on electron count and leading into the topic of resonance.

props.name: Presentation slides showing the nitrate ion molecule, valence electron calculations, the step-by-step Lewis structure construction, and the final structure with a double bond.

activities.description: The instructor explains the concept of resonance, using ozone (O3) as an example. He highlights the existence of multiple valid Lewis structures and emphasizes that the real molecule is a hybrid of these structures.

mood.description: The introduction of resonance challenges the viewer to think beyond single static structures and consider the dynamic nature of molecules.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene builds upon the previous example to formally introduce resonance and its implications for understanding molecular structure.

props.name: Presentation slides showing the two resonance structures of ozone and a textual explanation of resonance and hybrid structures.

scenes.thematicElements: Resonance, hybrid structures, Lewis structures, chemical bonding, ozone.
scenes.title: Introduction to Resonance

climax.description: The climax of the video occurs around the 03:33 timestamp in Scene 4 when the possibility of multiple correct Lewis structures for nitrate is introduced. This directly leads to the introduction of resonance in the following scene.

storylines.description:
The video primarily focuses on a single storyline:
Drawing Lewis Structures: This storyline progresses through the rules for drawing Lewis structures, including the need for double and triple bonds in specific cases. It then introduces the concept of resonance as a way to represent molecules with multiple valid Lewis structures.

trimmingSuggestions.description: Condensing the explanation of Rule 3 could make the introductory segment more concise.

Reducing the textual explanations and potentially incorporating animations to illustrate hybrid structures could make the resonance introduction more engaging.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Okay, on with part three from chapter one, and I'm not going through every slide.
I'm just hitting some highlights here. When it comes to covalent bonds, you won't be able to
put together molecules showing the presence or absence of double bonds or triple bonds.
Whenever those bonds show up, they are important, and so we want to know when they're called for.
If you've only got two or three atoms, like in the previous examples, you can draw them individually and just kind of connect the dots literally.
But when you have several atoms, and when there is the possibility of these extra bonds, the double and triple, it's not always obvious where they go.
So these rules will kind of step you through any problem that we would encounter when it comes to building molecules.
As it says in rule three, the connectivity has to be given. But apart from that, we can use these rules of valence electrons to come up with correct structures.
The octet rule is our constant guide, but there's always going to be a set number of electrons we can use to get us there.
So examples like this one for formaldehyde, off to the right is the calculation of how many valence electrons the whole molecule brings to the table.
I really don't care in my final answer which electrons came from carbon or oxygen. I just need the grand total.
And here that total is 12, six of which are already drawn. So if I build on top of this structure, as you see here, we can't get carbon and oxygen satisfied just by putting in pairs of dots.
We end up having to make a double bond between the carbon and the oxygen.
And like I say, we want to know when that's called for. So by knowing we can't use more than 12 electrons for this molecule.
And by knowing that I have to get carbon and oxygen to satisfy the octet, double bonds, the only thing that works.
Hydrogens are an easy case. They never make double bonds. They never have dots around them. They just make one single bond to get their two electrons.
This is another example where you don't have a whole lot of electrons to work with, but both that carbon and nitrogen need to satisfy the octet.
So this molecule only has 10 total. And if I consider the two bonds already shown, those have to be there. Plus putting those six dots around the nitrogen.
Well, almost done, but this carbon in the middle still isn't happy until we move those electrons off of nitrogen.
We're going to have to make a triple bond. Notice that gives eight electrons around both carbon and nitrogen.
And it does that using a grand total of 10. So we're constantly counting electrons and then distributing them.
Polyatomic ions like nitrate work the same way with the exception that negative charge, as you see, is an extra electron.
We have to put in our total. So whereas I would normally count 23 electrons for nitrate, that negative charge means there's 24.
If there were a positive charge up top here, we would have taken away an electron. And so atoms will make those adjustments when they can do something that's more stable.
And as I put in those electrons, I find that with 24 grand total, I'm going to have to put a double bond between nitrogen and one of those oxygens in order to get the octet.
Rule to be satisfied for all atoms. And that's what I'm trying to figure out. If I need a double bond, where can it go?
And in this case, as it says at the bottom, we've got a choice of where we make the double bond. So there's really three different answers.
And that leads into this next topic of resonance. Because when we have more than one way to draw the octet rule structure, we generally draw all the possibilities.
Because nitrate here really has three different answers that would satisfy our requirements.
Resonance is this phenomenon where we can draw more than one structure that obeys the octet rule. And it just changes the location of things like double bonds or triple bonds.
Ozone is a simple example of this because you can see those two structures are very similar, but the location of the double bond is different.
And as it says, we really want to draw both of these because the real answer to what ozone looks like is a hybrid of these two.
This next slide explains that as well. So being able to recognize the existence of resonance and when it occurs and how many structures we can draw,
that makes for good practice, but it also represents the reality of how these molecules are really made.
In real life, ozone doesn't have a short double bond and a long single bond. The real answer is somewhere in the middle. So we want to draw a structure to reflect that.
